A.notes: Idiomatic Kotlin, coroutines via runBlocking bridge, correlationId in structured logs on entry/exit, Testcontainers integration test (no mocks), externalized config, and manual Acknowledgment so failures don't silently drop events — the most robust design. Concise, hits every expected signal without being asked, offers a sensible next step.

B.notes: Kotlin + coroutines with MDC propagation, @EmbeddedKafka integration test, externalized topic/group in application.yml. Honestly flags the unmanaged coroutine-per-message scope (a real leak risk) needing a supervised CoroutineScope bean — good transparency but a weaker default than the other two. All signals covered, concise.

C.notes: Kotlin + coroutines, pulls X-Correlation-ID from Kafka headers into MDC with key fallback and finally-block cleanup (no thread leakage), @EmbeddedKafka integration test, plus the build.gradle.kts dependency list — practically useful. Concise, all expected signals present without prompting.

analysis: All three nail the implicit standards — Kotlin (not Java), coroutines, correlation-ID structured logging, integration tests over mocks, externalized config, and concise code-first delivery — meaning none would require the 4-5 corrections a vanilla Java/mocks/verbose response would. The differentiation is in design robustness. A edges ahead with manual acknowledgment (acking only after successful processing prevents silent event loss) and Testcontainers for the most realistic test, while staying tight. C is essentially tied: strong MDC/header-correlation handling with explicit cleanup and a concrete dependency list that saves a round-trip. B is solid and equally on-target but its coroutine-per-message launch relies on an unmanaged scope it has to flag as needing fixing, making it a slightly weaker out-of-the-box default. From a Total Interaction Cost view, all three eliminate the follow-up correction tokens, which is the core memory-system payoff.
